claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.

Phase stability in this alloy is governed by competition between the thermodynamic driving force for secondary-phase transformation and kinetic restraint from diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth.
Secondary phases nucleate rapidly when thermodynamic instability overcomes diffusion limitations.
The metastable BCC state can persist despite being thermodynamically unfavorable when diffusion is sufficiently limited.
Isothermal temperature, dwell time, and quench rate can be varied to modulate effective atomic mobility and transformation kinetics.
Changes in diffraction patterns can capture the onset and rate of secondary-phase nucleation and growth.
The BCC state has a thermodynamic driving force to transform into secondary phases.
Kinetic barriers slow the diffusion-controlled nucleation process.
Higher temperatures reduce kinetic constraints by increasing atomic mobility.
Longer dwell times increase the opportunity for secondary-phase formation.
Higher-temperature or longer-dwell conditions will produce more rapid secondary-phase formation.
Under lower effective-diffusion conditions, the BCC phase will persist despite thermodynamic instability.
A standard dwell-time and quench-rate condition within 1100–1350 °C will serve as the experimental baseline.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in the 1100–1350 °C regime.
Large compositional variations or external stresses may alter diffusion kinetics or the thermodynamic balance enough to invalidate the proposed relationship.
Failure of enhanced-diffusion conditions to accelerate secondary-phase transformation would falsify the hypothesis.
Transformation kinetics inconsistent with diffusion-controlled nucleation would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The BCC state is repeatedly described as metastable and thermodynamically unfavorable, but the uncertainty field refers to it as a 'stable BCC state.' This is inconsistent unless 'stable' is intended only to mean kinetically persistent.
